mamba runtime: Phase A opaque-value boundary inventory gate before token cutover
records.body:
## Goal

### Dependencies

- Epic owner: #1996; closed #2024 remains historical architecture evidence.
- Production dependency: none. This Phase A gate blocks typed-token leaves #3118, #3228, and #3639.

Make omissions in the opaque-value census deterministic red before the tag-6 typed-token cutover. This is characterization/test tooling only. CPython E2E is not applicable to a static provenance gate; the independent oracle is a frozen mutation corpus whose cases must each fail for their own diagnostic.

## How

### Allowed artifact boundary

The implementation boundary is limited to:

- `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/opaque_value_boundary.py`
- `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/fixtures/opaque_value_boundary/*`
- `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/inventory.toml`
- `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/expected.toml`
- focused runner/fixture files under `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/`

Reuse `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/rust_scan.py` and `provenance.py`; do not build a regex-only parallel scanner. The inventory classifies each stable site as `producer`, `consumer`, `registry`, `classifier`, `private_metadata`, or `python_numeric`, with disposition `legacy_debt`, `typed_token`, `private_only`, or `python_numeric`, plus kind/family/parent route and rationale.

The verifier red conditions are: unclassified discovery; stale/duplicate/moved/digest-drifted row; raw opaque producer misclassified as numeric/private; `as_int` flow into table/class/ownership/threshold/first-live consumers without a declared route; private metadata reified into generic `MbValue`; new production file not covered; and typed-token enablement while legacy debt remains.

Frozen mutations cover direct/hidden producers, direct/helper table lookup, threshold classifier, first-live multi-registry probe, private-slot reification, new source file, moved/stale row, plus positive UID/GID/index and confined metadata controls. Unknown flow is `needs_classification`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Focused scanner self-tests prove comment/string masking, incomplete-delimiter rejection, stable semantic IDs, bounded helper/assignment flow, and unseen temporary-fixture handling.
- [ ] Every frozen negative mutation fails with its own stable expected diagnostic; positive numeric/private controls remain green.
- [ ] Current-tree `inventory` mode is green only when every discovered site is classified and no listed legacy site silently grows/moves/drifts.
- [ ] `typed_only` is automatically selected by the production discriminator in a future phase and would currently fail because legacy debt is nonzero; it is not a manual flag.
- [ ] The ledger includes the confirmed `OsSurrogateFd` and `EvalExecFunction` families and all other classified core/stdlib families; unresolved weakref/identity flows remain blockers rather than guessed safe.
- [ ] A fresh self-check plus governance-gate run confirms the scanner remains within its declared boundary and changes no shipping behavior.

## Never

- Do not accept import-only, mock-only, sentinel-only, broad normalization, swallowed failure, implicit fallback, xfail, a skipped/ungraded row, or one lucky green run as completion.
- Do not infer completion from ticket metadata, prose status, focused test, historical scratch output, or an unidentified binary.
- Do not widen a production seam or absorb a newly discovered defect beyond the named production seam.
- Do not modify `apps/mamba/src/**`, Cargo configuration, existing audit semantics, CPython fixtures/manifests, kind codes, tag encoding, or any typed-token production path in Phase A.

<!-- mamba-t1-tune:start -->
## T1 Epic Dispatch Review

- Epic owner: #1996.
- Review verdict: `readiness:needs-contract`.
- Why contract work remains: the issue is bounded in intent, but it is not yet a zero-decision worker packet.
- Reference seam only; these paths are not a write authorization while `readiness:needs-contract`:
  - `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/opaque_value_boundary.py`
  - `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/fixtures/opaque_value_boundary/*`
  - `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/inventory.toml`
  - `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/expected.toml`
  - `apps/mamba/tests/governance/gates/t1_opaque_value_boundary/`
  - `apps/mamba/tools/ownership/rust_scan.py`
  - `apps/mamba/src/**`
- Controller must: remove apps/mamba/src/** from the write allowlist, name the exact scanner commands, and bind the current inventory/expected files to digests.
- Release condition: the controller must add the missing frozen inputs to this issue, independently reproduce them on canonical `app/mamba`, and then change the readiness label.
- Dispatch rule: no implementation or production edit is allowed while this issue is `readiness:needs-contract`. Evidence-only inspection must also stop before a write.
- Stop rule: if the frozen evidence names a different seam, result, or oracle, report `BLOCKED_DISCOVERY` on this issue and stop.
- Tracker rule: an implementation worker must not create, split, atomize, amend, close, or relabel issues. Only the controller owns tracker changes and acceptance.

<!-- mamba-t1-tune:end -->

records.title: [Feature]: Add Postgres benchmark suite measuring CRUD performance at scale
records.body:
### Problem statement

olonyCore currently lacks comprehensive performance benchmarks for Postgres-backed entity operations at realistic production scales. While functional parity has been achieved across memory, SQLite, and Postgres stores with >90% test coverage, we have no quantitative data on:

- CRUD operation throughput at scale (10K, 100K, 1M entities)
- Query performance for complex relationship traversals
- Join performance for normalized schema
- Index effectiveness for common access patterns
- Transaction overhead and isolation level impact
- Comparison baseline between SQLite and Postgres at different scales

Without this data, operators cannot make informed decisions about storage backend selection, capacity planning, or performance optimization. This is particularly critical as entity counts grow in production deployments.

### Proposed change

Implement a comprehensive Postgres benchmark suite that:

1. **CRUD Operations**: Measure Create, Read, Update, Delete throughput at 10K, 100K, and 1M entity scales
2. **Relationship Operations**: Benchmark relationship traversals, including:
   - Colony → Subject → Assignment chains
   - Protocol → ProtocolStep fan-out queries
   - Lineage ancestry/descendant queries
3. **Batch Operations**: Test bulk insert/update/delete performance
4. **Concurrent Access**: Measure performance under concurrent read/write workloads
5. **Index Impact**: Validate index effectiveness for declared unique and indexed fields
6. **Storage Comparison**: Provide SQLite vs. Postgres comparison at each scale tier

Benchmarks should:
- Use Go's `testing.B` framework for consistency
- Generate realistic fixture data using existing synthetic fixture infrastructure
- Report percentile latencies (p50, p95, p99) in addition to throughput
- Integrate with CI for regression detection (with reasonable time limits)
- Produce machine-readable output for trend analysis

### CRUD scope

Create, Read, Update, Delete

### Governing RFC or ADR

ADR-0003, ADR-0007

### Impacted areas

- [ ] Core lifecycle & state machines
- [ ] API & client contracts
- [x] Data storage & persistence
- [x] Operator tooling / CLI
- [ ] Documentation & RFCs
- [ ] Plugins & integrations
- [x] Observability & telemetry

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Given a Postgres instance, when running `make bench-postgres`, then CRUD benchmarks execute at 10K, 100K, and 1M entity scales
- [ ] Benchmark suite covers all 16 entity types from entity-model.json
- [ ] Relationship traversal benchmarks cover at least 5 common query patterns
- [ ] Results include throughput (ops/sec), latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and memory usage
- [ ] Comparison benchmarks between SQLite and Postgres at each scale tier
- [ ] CI integration with reasonable runtime limits (<10 minutes for smoke tests)
- [ ] Documentation includes performance baselines and capacity planning guidance
- [ ] Benchmarks use realistic fixture data from `testutil/fixtures/entity-model/`

### Risks & dependencies

- Large-scale benchmarks may require significant CI resources or external test infrastructure
- Postgres configuration (connection pooling, work_mem, etc.) will significantly impact results - must document baseline configuration
- Fixture generation at 1M scale may require memory-efficient streaming approaches
- Consider cost/time trade-off for CI integration (perhaps run full benchmarks on-demand rather than every commit)
- Should establish performance SLOs before implementation to guide optimization efforts

### Compliance affirmations

- [x] This proposal does not contradict any accepted RFCs or ADRs.
- [x] The proposal aligns with the core lifecycle and state machine contracts.

### Additional context

This feature supports v0.2.0 objectives for production readiness and operational confidence. It builds on:

- Triple store parity established in Entity Model v0 (memory/SQLite/Postgres)
- Synthetic fixtures at `testutil/fixtures/entity-model/snapshot.json`
- Existing Postgres DDL at `docs/schema/sql/entity_model.postgres.sql`
- ADR-0007 storage baseline with env-based driver selection

Related infrastructure:
- `internal/persistence/` - store implementations
- `testutil/fixtures/` - fixture generation
- `Makefile` - integration point for new bench target

Performance baselines will inform future optimization work and help identify scalability bottlenecks before they impact production deployments.

records.title: fix(deps): eliminate vulnerable desktop GTK3 transitive dependencies
records.body:
## Problem and impact

A checksum-verified OSV-Scanner 2.4.0 scan of `apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.lock` identified one distinct medium-severity Rust memory-safety advisory and sixteen unmaintained-crate advisories in the current desktop dependency graph. OSV reports the memory-safety advisory twice under its RustSec and GitHub aliases, so the raw output contains eighteen records representing seventeen distinct advisories.

The medium finding is RUSTSEC-2024-0429 / GHSA-wrw7-89jp-8q8g in `glib` 0.18.5. The affected iterator implementation is fixed in `glib` 0.20.0. The current lock reaches `glib` 0.18.5 through the Linux GTK3 dependency chain selected by Tauri 2.11.5, which is already the current reviewed Tauri crate release. Application source does not call the named iterator directly, but native call analysis was unavailable in the audit environment, so runtime reachability has not been established or ruled out.

The remaining advisories identify unmaintained GTK3 bindings, `proc-macro-error`, and UNIC crates. These do not carry vulnerability severity by themselves, but they increase the cost and uncertainty of future security maintenance.

This blocks release readiness for a supported Linux desktop artifact until the vulnerable path is removed, safely patched, or subject to an evidence-backed, time-bounded risk decision.

## Scope

- `apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`
- Tauri, Wry, Tao, WebKitGTK, GTK, GLib, URL-pattern, and macro transitive chains
- Linux desktop build and packaging prerequisites
- Native dependency scanning, SBOMs, support policy, and release-candidate evidence
- Desktop security, navigation, IPC, credentials, notifications, update, and rollback verification

## Non-sensitive evidence

- Direct desktop dependency: Tauri 2.11.5.
- Representative path: `nexa-desktop` -> `tauri` -> `gtk` 0.18.2 -> `glib` 0.18.5.
- Additional paths reach GTK3 bindings through `tauri-runtime-wry`, `wry`, `tao`, and `webkit2gtk`.
- The URL-pattern path reaches five unmaintained UNIC crates through `tauri-utils` and `urlpattern`.
- OSV-Scanner 2.4.0 was downloaded from the official release, verified against its published SHA-256 list, and run recursively against the exact lock.
- npm audits and GitHub dependency alerts remain clean; those tools do not replace Cargo advisory review.

## Technical requirements

- Reproduce the inventory with current OSV and RustSec data and deduplicate aliases.
- Establish target-specific dependency paths for Linux, macOS, and Windows.
- Determine whether the affected `glib::VariantStrIter` implementation is reachable in the supported Linux binary using native call analysis plus manual review.
- Prefer an upstream Tauri/WebKitGTK/GTK migration that removes `glib` below 0.20. If that is unavailable, evaluate a narrowly maintained backport without changing public crate identity or weakening lock integrity.
- Do not add a broad advisory ignore. Any temporary exception must identify the exact advisory and package, owner, evidence, compensating controls, expiry, and release decision.
- Replace or explicitly disposition each unmaintained dependency chain.
- Keep direct and transitive versions, registry sources, checksums, features, and platform conditions reproducible.
- Add a native dependency gate that distinguishes vulnerabilities from informational maintenance advisories and fails closed on unreviewed vulnerability data.

## Security and privacy requirements

- Preserve the desktop navigation allowlist, content security policy, typed IPC boundary, capability minimization, credential isolation, notification privacy, and update signature boundary.
- Do not solve the dependency finding by enabling unnecessary Tauri features, widening native capabilities, disabling platform protections, or suppressing all Rust advisories.
- Scanner, build, and crash output must not expose credentials, filesystem secrets, private notification data, or user content.

## Testing requirements

- Run OSV and RustSec-compatible scans against the resolved Cargo lock and produced platform SBOMs.
- Run `cargo test`, `cargo clippy` with warnings denied, formatting, feature-unification review, duplicate review, and native call analysis on a supported Rust toolchain.
- Build and package supported Linux, macOS, and Windows targets and verify their exact dependency inventories.
- Re-run desktop navigation, IPC schema, credential persistence, notification privacy, deep-link, update, rollback, corruption, and recovery tests.
- Run production web/server checks to prove the desktop dependency change does not alter shared contracts.
- Retain exact commit, lock, toolchain, platform, architecture, artifact, scan, and SBOM evidence.

## Operational and documentation requirements

- Document the selected migration or backport, support impact, system prerequisites, rollout order, monitoring, and rollback.
- Update the security audit, threat model residual-risk register, compatibility policy, desktop prerequisites, and release-candidate checklist.
- If an upstream dependency blocks remediation, record the upstream reference and review the block at least monthly until resolved.

## Dependencies

Coordinate with desktop and release work in #97-#104, #117, and #118. The repository currently uses the latest reviewed Tauri crate, so an upstream platform migration or a separately reviewed patch may be required.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The medium `glib` advisory is absent from every supported desktop artifact, or a repository-owner-approved exception has exact reachability evidence, compensating controls, an expiry, and an explicit release decision.
- [ ] Every unmaintained crate advisory is removed or has a documented owner, migration target, and review deadline.
- [ ] No broad OSV, RustSec, package, path, or severity suppression is introduced.
- [ ] Native tests, Clippy, platform builds, packaging, desktop security tests, update/rollback tests, and production shared-contract checks pas

## Problem
`dbt/models/marts/fct_policy_optimization.sql` is not part of the production pipeline and depends on test/demo variables. Repository tests explicitly describe it as stale scaffolding.

Leaving a fact-named mart in this state makes the supported data model ambiguous and risks accidental selection in ad hoc dbt runs.

## Decision required
Either remove the stale model and its references, or redesign and integrate it as a documented production mart with real inputs, build ordering, schema contracts, and consumers.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The repository makes an explicit keep/remove decision.
- [ ] If removed: delete stale model/tests/docs references without affecting optimizer outputs.
- [ ] If retained: replace test-only variables, add it to the correct build path, document schema/lineage, and add dbt tests.
- [ ] Production dbt selection contains no orphan fact model.
- [ ] Validation uses an isolated database.

records.title: (USED CHATGPT!!) here's good criticise
records.body:
I think **LLM Context is one of the more thoughtfully designed context-management tools** I've seen. It's solving a real bottleneck rather than trying to be "yet another AI framework."

What I like most is that it changes the unit of work from **"send files"** to **"describe the task."**

Instead of saying:

> Here are 27 files...

you say:

> "Debug OAuth"

and a rule determines the relevant context. That's a much more scalable abstraction.

### The strongest ideas

**1. Rule composition**

The filter/instruction/style/excerpt separation is excellent.

Instead of one giant prompt, you build prompts like software:

* authentication instructions
* Python style
* repository exclusions
* excerpt strategy

and compose them.

That scales extremely well.

---

**2. Context isn't static**

Most people treat context like this:

```
project/
    send everything
```

LLM Context treats context like

```
Task
↓
Rule
↓
Relevant files
↓
Relevant excerpts
↓
LLM
```

That's a huge improvement.

---

**3. MCP integration**

This is probably the biggest feature.

Instead of interrupting the conversation with

> "Can you upload auth.py?"

the model can ask for it through MCP.

That makes conversations much more natural.

---

**4. Preview**

I love

```
lc-preview
```

before actually sending.

One of the biggest wastes in AI workflows is realizing halfway through:

> Oops... that included 40MB.

Previewing token size is underrated.

---

**5. Excerpting instead of full files**

Very smart.

Many files contain

* imports
* comments
* blank lines
* boilerplate

that contribute almost nothing.

Sending structural excerpts first is often enough.

---

## Where I think it falls short

### It still depends on humans writing rules

This is the biggest limitation.

Suppose I ask

> "Optimize rendering performance."

Someone has to create

```
tmp-prm-performance
```

If the rule misses

```
renderer.ts
```

the AI never sees it.

Ideally the AI should infer most of that automatically.

---

### Doesn't reason about code graph

Imagine this:

```
Scene.tsx

imports

Renderer.ts

imports

Shader.ts

imports

WebGLManager.ts
```

If your task touches Scene,

I'd want the tool to automatically include the dependency graph.

Current rule systems usually don't.

---

### No semantic retrieval

Imagine I ask

> "Find where XP gets awarded."

A keyword search misses

```
grantExperience()
```

```
rewardProgress()
```

```
incrementLevel()
```

A semantic index would find them.

This tool doesn't appear to build one.

---

### No architecture awareness

I'd love something like

```
lc-impact login
```

↓

```
17 files affected

4 APIs

3 database tables

2 tests

1 UI component
```

That would be incredible.

---

### Static instead of adaptive

Imagine the conversation goes

AI:

> Show me auth.

↓

User sends auth.

↓

AI realizes

> Actually I need session middleware too.

↓

Needs another request.

I'd rather the context evolve automatically based on the conversation.

---

## For your project (Jusoor)

Ironically, your project is exactly where this shines.

You have

* frontend
* backend
* AI prompts
* NPC system
* world graph
* scenario engine
* voice
* analytics
* auth
* social hub

No LLM should receive all of that.

Imagine rules like

```
prm-scenario-engine

prm-world-map

prm-social-feed

prm-auth

prm-performance

prm-rendering

prm-audio

prm-mobile

prm-localization
```

Each would expose only 5–20 files instead of hundreds.

That would noticeably improve response quality and reduce context waste.

---

## If I were building "LLM Context v2"

I'd add five capabilities:

* A dependency graph (imports, callers, callees) so related files are pulled in automatically.
* Semantic search over symbols and behavior, not just filenames or paths.
* Automatic impact analysis showing which modules, APIs, and tests are likely affected by a change.
* Conversation-aware context that expands as the model discovers new dependencies instead of relying on fixed rules.
* Repository embeddings and architecture metadata so the tool understands concepts like "NPC pipeline" or "rendering engine" rather than only files.

---

### Overall rating

* **Concept:** 10/10
* **Architecture:** 9.5/10
* **Developer experience:** 9/10
* **Scalability:** 9/10
* **Novelty:** 8/10 (it's an excellent implementation of ideas that have been emerging around prompt engineering and context management rather than a fundamentally new paradigm)

The repository feels like it was built by someone who has spent a lot of time working with large codebases and LLMs. It focuses on reducing friction instead of adding another abstraction layer.

That said, I think the next generation of these tools will shift from **rule-based context selection** to **repository intelligence**—where the system understands symbols, dependency graphs, architecture, and the evolving conversation, and can decide what context to fetch with minimal human configuration. That's the direction I'd expect tools in this space to evolve over the next few years.

records.title: [P1][Transformation][Data] Define reusable Silver/Gold transformation framework and engine selection
records.body:
## Background
#70 defines the Medallion target architecture, while #71 standardizes heterogeneous source onboarding. The remaining gap is how data is transformed from Bronze into reusable Silver datasets and business-ready Gold data products.

Beluga already contains Flink, Airflow, Trino, and the new DuckDB path. Without explicit transformation boundaries, each data product may choose an engine ad hoc, creating inconsistent quality, lineage, operational, and resource characteristics.

## Goal
Define a common transformation framework that selects Flink, Airflow/SQL, DuckDB, or Trino based on workload semantics, scale, latency, statefulness, and concurrency.

## Requirements
- Define transformation categories: streaming/stateful, batch SQL, lightweight local/bounded SQL, enrichment/join, aggregation, data-quality remediation, and Gold data-product publishing.
- Define deterministic engine-selection rules for Flink, Airflow/SQL, DuckDB, and Trino.
- Keep transformation logic version-controlled and reproducible.
- Define dependency and promotion rules between Bronze, Silver, and Gold datasets.
- Define incremental transformation, idempotency, checkpointing, retry, and backfill semantics.
- Support quarantine/reject paths for invalid Silver records without silently losing source data.
- Define schema compatibility and contract checks before publishing downstream layers.
- Capture transformation metadata: source snapshot/version, code version, runtime version, execution timestamp, job/run identifier, and output dataset version.
- Preserve end-to-end lineage and quality evidence through transformations.
- Define Gold publication rules for BI/reporting/AI use cases and prevent uncontrolled direct consumption of raw Bronze data.
- Integrate with #63 routing and #65 benchmark evidence so engine choice is measurable rather than subjective.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Transformation classes and engine-selection decision matrix are documented.
- [ ] At least one representative Silver pipeline runs with each applicable execution mode.
- [ ] Incremental/retry/backfill behavior is deterministic.
- [ ] Transformation output carries reproducible lineage and source/runtime metadata.
- [ ] Silver quality and schema gates block invalid publication according to policy.
- [ ] Gold publication produces governed, queryable datasets consumable by Trino and DuckDB.
- [ ] A workload can be migrated between supported engines without changing the resulting data contract.

## Related Issues
- #12 performance/capacity SLOs
- #19 lineage and metadata quality
- #20 data quality gates
- #22 interface contracts
- #61 DuckDB complementary analytics engine
- #63 workload routing and Trino fallback
- #65 Trino/DuckDB consistency benchmark
- #70 Medallion architecture
- #71 heterogeneous source onboarding
